keyVerseText: The other disciples therefore said unto him, We have seen the Lord. But he said unto them, Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.
rootMeaning: The Greek noun τύπος (týpos) derives from the verb τύπτω (týptō), which means to strike, beat, or smite. This root emphasizes the idea of an impression or mark made by a blow, such as a stamp or print. Unlike general terms for striking, τύπος conveys the lasting effect or form left by an impact, highlighting the tangible result of being struck rather than the act of striking itself.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, τύπος appears sixteen times and is translated variously as 'the print,' 'ensamples,' 'figures,' 'manner,' and 'examples,' among others. This range shows its use both in literal senses—such as the physical imprint of nails—and in figurative senses, like patterns or models for imitation. The word thus bridges concrete physical impressions and abstract ethical or doctrinal patterns, revealing its flexibility in conveying both tangible and spiritual realities.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding τύπος as a mark or pattern formed by a decisive blow enriches our grasp of biblical typology and Christ’s redemptive work. It reminds believers that Christ’s crucifixion left an indelible mark—both physically in His resurrected body and spiritually as the ultimate pattern for faith and obedience. This concept underscores the reality that God’s purposes are not abstract but are stamped into history and the believer’s life, calling Christians to follow the example and form revealed in Christ. The word also highlights the continuity between Old Testament types and their fulfillment in the New Testament, affirming the unity and divine design of Scripture.
keyVerseReflection: John 20:25 recounts Thomas’s doubt until he personally sees and touches 'the print of the nails' in Jesus’ hands. The use of τύπος here powerfully conveys the tangible, physical evidence of Christ’s crucifixion—an indelible mark that authenticates His resurrection. This impression is not merely a memory or symbol but a real, lasting proof that invites faith grounded in encounter with the risen Lord. It teaches us that the marks of Christ’s suffering are central to Christian belief, assuring us of the reality of His victory over death.
